extracted.intended_audience: U.S. policymakers, patent practitioners, inventors, and industry stakeholders
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation and description of policy and procedural standards proposed in S.23 (the America Invents Act) relating to patent priority (first-to-file), prior art, post-grant review, USPTO funding, and related patent-system mechanics in the United States.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty of proving copying in derivation proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the bill’s system, proving that someone copied an invention (derivation) is difficult because there is no discovery in derivation proceedings and the first inventor will not have access to the alleged copier’s documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because derivation proceedings provide no discovery, a first inventor cannot typically obtain the documents needed to show another applicant derived their application from the first inventor; this increases difficulty of proving a claim of derivation and is cited as a substantive problem with FITF-style derivation processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-to-file incentives and risk of overfiling
rubrics_metrics.description: First-to-file incentivizes inventors to race to the Patent Office to protect ideas as quickly as possible, which will likely result in significant overfiling of dead-end inventions and burden the PTO and small inventors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policymakers should weigh whether FITF's race-to-file incentives will increase low-quality filings and administrative burden versus benefits of harmonization and predictability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interference proceeding frequency as empirical measure
rubrics_metrics.description: Disputes about who is first to invent are resolved now in interference proceedings, which number only about 50 a year out of 480,000 patent applications (a very small percentage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the low incidence of interferences as evidence that first-to-invent problems are rare; consider empirical rates when assessing the need for systemic change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost of proving first-to-invent vs provisional filing
rubrics_metrics.description: Proving first-to-invent in disputes typically costs at least $400,000 in legal fees (even more on appeal), whereas establishing a filing date through a provisional application costs about $110.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare litigation costs against inexpensive procedural options (e.g., provisional filings) when evaluating the practical impact of changing priority rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-inventor-to-file (FITF) simplification & harmonization
rubrics_metrics.description: Moving to a first-inventor-to-file system simplifies the process of acquiring rights, reduces legal costs, improves fairness, and supports U.S. innovators competing globally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments in favor stress international harmonization, objectivity, and reduced complexity; assess benefits against potential harms (e.g., racing to file, reduced protection for small inventors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit prior art to public disclosures and earlier-filed applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Limit 'prior art' used to bar a patent from issuing to only those disclosures made available to the public before the patent was sought and disclosures in earlier-filed patent applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This narrows the scope of actionable prior art compared to uses of secret or foreign secret activities; consider retrospective effects on existing practices and on the one-year 'grace period' concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliminate arcane and subjective tests; make rules objective
rubrics_metrics.description: Remove arcane and subjective tests for deciding whether to issue a patent and replace them with simple, transparent, objective standards to make patenting rules more predictable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reform should favor clarity and predictability in patentability determinations; evaluate proposed statutory language and PTO examination practices for objectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeal patent interference provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeal the 'patent interference' provisions that inject delay, cost and uncertainty into the patenting process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eliminating interferences is promoted as reducing litigation and administrative burden; examine replacement mechanisms (e.g., derivation proceedings) and their procedural safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public submissions to assist examination (third-party pre-grant submissions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let members of the public provide patent examiners with relevant publications and other public documents before deciding whether a patent can be granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create processes and timing rules for third-party submissions so examiners can consider public prior art early; ensure mechanisms are not abused and include limits and procedures for submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-grant review to assure patent quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Permit members of the public to challenge whether newly issued patents meet each of the rigorous standards for patenting and require the USPTO to promptly cancel any patents that do not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post-grant review is presented as an important new mechanism to assure patent quality; assess thresholds, estoppel effects, and timelines for prompt resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplemental examination before enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorize supplemental examination proceedings, before a patent is enforced, to allow patent owners to present the USPTO with information that may be used to assure the scope of the patent is commensurate with its contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supplemental examination can reduce inequitable conduct and clarify patent scope prior to enforcement; evaluate procedures, costs, and strategic uses by patentees.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO fee-setting authority and sufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow the USPTO to set fees for processing patent applications sufficient to cover the costs of promptly completing a high-quality examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Granting fee-setting authority aims to align resources with workload and improve examination quality and timeliness; consider safeguards, transparency, and fee structures to avoid undue burden on small entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit false patent marking damages
rubrics_metrics.description: Limit the ability of a party to recover false patent marking to the amount of the party’s actual competitive injuries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This narrows potential treble or statutory damages remedies for false marking claims; weigh deterrence benefits versus risk of excessive damages litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strengthen grace period and prevent interloping
rubrics_metrics.description: Make an inventor’s public disclosure a bar to others thereafter patenting that work or obvious variations and secure the one-year 'grace period' so that a U.S. inventor’s disclosure preserves their own ability to patent during the year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: S.23 is described as 'bulletproofing' the grace period and reversing 1994 WTO impacts that enabled foreign secret prior activities to undercut U.S. disclosures; analyze retroactivity and international compatibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliminate use of dates-of-invention for validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Put an end to any use of 'dates of invention' to determine whether a U.S. patent is valid or not, and strip out grounds for invalidating a U.S. patent based on secret activities undertaken by inventors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Removing date-of-invention inquiries simplifies validity analysis but shifts emphasis to filing/public disclosure dates; examine effects on inventors who relied on prior-date proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTO funding lockbox / revolving fund to prevent fee diversion
rubrics_metrics.description: Create a lockbox—a new revolving fund at the Treasury—where user fees paid to the PTO go directly into the revolving fund for PTO operations so Congress cannot divert those fees to other general revenue purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aims to ensure PTO has consistent resources to reduce backlog and pendency; consider oversight, accountability, and whether fee revenues will be adequate and appropriately used.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTO performance and workload metrics (backlog & pendency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Key performance metrics cited: first action pendency ~26 months, total overall pendency ~35 months, total pending patent applications over 1.16 million, with over 718,000 waiting for first action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these quantitative metrics to justify funding and structural reforms; any reform should include targets and monitoring to reduce backlog and pendency and improve examination throughput.
